scope: Independent educational pilot pathway, not official RAKIURA onboarding and not a validated research qualification.

stages.name: 01 · Start with a real binary
stages.question: When is a binary gravitationally bound, and what makes its orbit change?
stages.researchTask: For a bound point-mass binary, compare the orbital energies at a and 2a and explain why eccentricity affects pericentre without changing energy at fixed a.
stages.deliverable: A one-page orbit-energy argument, with a labeled diagram and explicit assumptions.

stages.name: 02 · Follow the progenitor stars
stages.question: How can interactions between two massive stars alter the compact remnants they leave?
stages.researchTask: Compare two toy mass-transfer histories and list what is needed to infer final separation. Distinguish a mass ledger from an orbital-angular-momentum budget.
stages.deliverable: A two-column comparison of evolutionary mechanisms and stated model limitations.

stages.name: 03 · Test compact-binary survival
stages.question: Can a supernova turn the same initial binary into a survivor or an unbound pair?
stages.researchTask: For fixed separation and post-explosion masses, vary kick orientation and compute specific orbital energy to classify whether a surviving binary is bound.
stages.deliverable: A table of toy post-supernova orbital energies with reasoning about kick direction.

stages.name: 04 · Connect the merger to its waveform
stages.question: Why does the emitted wave chirp, and what does its phase reveal?
stages.researchTask: Derive the equal-mass chirp-mass expression and connect an increasing orbital frequency to the increasing dominant GW frequency.
stages.deliverable: A worked derivation that distinguishes observed detector-frame masses from source-frame masses.

stages.name: 05 · Model a population, not one anecdote
stages.question: How do sampled initial binaries become a distribution of merger candidates?
stages.researchTask: Generate a transparent toy sample, count distinct systems rather than event rows, record the seed and normalize a selected yield by the stated sample denominator.
stages.deliverable: A reproducible toy-data analysis with sampling assumptions and an uncertainty paragraph.

stages.name: 06 · Confront a detected population
stages.question: Which progenitor assumptions are constrained by detections after selection effects and cosmic delays?
stages.researchTask: Compare a two-class intrinsic population with its expected detected catalog, showing how detection efficiency changes apparent class fractions.
stages.deliverable: A brief research memo distinguishing formation, merger, detection and inference assumptions.

problems.title: Derive the circular-binary binding-energy expression
problems.scenario: Two Newtonian point masses m₁ and m₂ orbit their common center of mass on a circular orbit with separation a.
problems.task: Starting from force balance for relative motion and the reduced mass, derive E = −Gm₁m₂/(2a). Explain which assumptions would fail during a common-envelope episode.
steps: Write μ=m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂) for the reduced mass and M=m₁+m₂ for total mass.
Relative circular motion obeys μv_rel²/a=Gm₁m₂/a², hence v_rel²=GM/a.
K=μv_rel²/2=Gm₁m₂/(2a) and U=−Gm₁m₂/a.
Add K+U=−Gm₁m₂/(2a); a dissipative envelope can exchange orbital energy with gas.
rubric: Scope of isolated point-mass assumptions identified

problems.title: Compare two equal natal kicks with different directions
problems.scenario: In toy units, immediately after mass loss r=1, GM_final=1, and the pre-kick relative speed is 1 along the +y direction. A kick of magnitude 0.5 is applied parallel or antiparallel to the motion.
problems.task: Compute the new relative speed and ε=v²/2−GM/r for both cases. Classify binding and explain why magnitude alone is insufficient.
steps: Parallel: v=1.5, so ε=1.5²/2−1=+0.125; this toy post-event orbit is unbound.
Antiparallel: v=0.5, so ε=0.5²/2−1=−0.875; this toy orbit is bound.
Separation is frozen during the instantaneous impulse; changing the kick direction changes the post-event relative kinetic energy.
To infer eccentricity also compute angular momentum from r × v and the updated gravitational parameter.

problems.title: Audit a non-conservative mass-transfer budget
problems.scenario: A donor of 12 M☉ loses 4 M☉, while its 6 M☉ companion accretes 3 M☉.
problems.task: Calculate final masses and lost mass, then explain precisely why the separation cannot be deduced from this ledger alone.
steps: The donor ends at 8 M☉ and the accretor at 9 M☉.
One solar mass leaves the binary, so the episode is non-conservative.
The orbital response depends on angular momentum carried by lost material and other exchanges as well as on mass redistribution.
A transfer-stability conclusion additionally requires stellar structure and Roche-lobe response.

problems.title: Simplify chirp mass for two equal masses
problems.scenario: Two compact objects have equal source-frame masses m₁=m₂=m. The chirp-mass definition is M_c=(m₁m₂)^(3/5)/(m₁+m₂)^(1/5).
problems.task: Derive M_c=m/2^(1/5), compute it for m=10 M☉, and state how detector-frame mass differs at redshift z.
steps: Substitute m₁=m₂=m: numerator (m²)^(3/5)=m^(6/5).
Cancel powers to obtain m/2^(1/5)≈0.87055m, hence ≈8.71 M☉ for m=10 M☉.
At redshift z, the waveform constrains M_c,det=(1+z)M_c,source; this is redshift of the waveform, not physical growth of source mass.

problems.title: Distinguish event rows from distinct simulated binaries
problems.scenario: A toy event log contains IDs [4,4,8,8,8,10]. Only systems 8 and 10 reach the specified merger outcome, and their sampling weights are 2 and 5.
problems.task: Count event rows and distinct simulated systems, calculate the raw success fraction and weighted success yield, then identify which normalization is missing for a physical formation efficiency.
steps: There are 6 recorded events but only 3 distinct sampled binaries: 4, 8 and 10.
Two out of three distinct systems succeed, giving an unweighted toy fraction 2/3.
The weighted successful-system yield is 2+5=7 arbitrary weight units.
A mass-normalized formation efficiency additionally requires the represented formed stellar mass and a consistent sampling-weight convention.
rubric: Distinct IDs counted rather than rows

problems.title: Recover the meaning of a selection-biased catalog
problems.scenario: Two astrophysical classes have equal intrinsic expected counts, 100 each. A search detects class A with probability 0.8 and B with probability 0.2.
problems.task: Find expected observed counts, compare observed and intrinsic ratios, and explain why simply reading the detected catalog can mislead formation-channel inference.
steps: Expected detected A=100×0.8=80 and B=100×0.2=20.
The intrinsic class ratio is 1:1, whereas the expected detected ratio is 4:1.
Detected counts must be compared to a forward prediction that includes the selection function.
An actual GW rate estimate also requires sensitive spacetime volume, observation time, measurement uncertainty and the population likelihood.
rubric: Limits of simple inverse weighting stated

problems.title: Recover orbital shape from the two turning points
problems.scenario: A Newtonian two-body orbit has relative pericentre distance r_p=3 toy length units and apocentre distance r_a=9. The orbital ellipse is Keplerian and neither mass changes during an orbit.
problems.task: Calculate semi-major axis and eccentricity, then explain whether two ellipses with the same a but different e can have the same total orbital energy.
steps: Use r_p=a(1−e) and r_a=a(1+e), so r_p+r_a=2a and a=(3+9)/2=6.
Subtract the equations: r_a−r_p=2ae, giving e=(9−3)/(9+3)=1/2.
For fixed m₁ and m₂, E=−Gm₁m₂/(2a); eccentricity changes angular momentum and turning points but not this energy at fixed a.
Identify the limitations: point masses, Newtonian potential and a bound Kepler ellipse, not a dissipative stellar interaction.
rubric: Energy interpretation distinguished from orbital shape

problems.title: A purely radial impulse can change orbit shape without increasing angular momentum
problems.scenario: Consider the relative orbit immediately after an impulsive event. Set r=(1,0), GM_after=1, and start from v=(0,1) in dimensionless Newtonian units. Apply an instantaneous radial velocity impulse Δv=(0.3,0).
problems.task: Compute the new specific energy and angular momentum magnitude. Decide whether the new orbit remains bound and explain why the radial impulse changes energy but not angular momentum about the origin.
steps: After the impulse v′=(0.3,1), so |v′|²=0.3²+1²=1.09.
The specific orbital energy is ε=1.09/2−1=−0.455, so the post-event orbit is bound in this model.
The specific angular momentum h=|r×v′|=|1×1−0×0.3|=1; the radial velocity component contributes no cross product at the instant of impulse.
The new eccentricity follows e²=1+2εh²/(GM_after)²=1−0.91=0.09, hence e=0.3. State that the event is instantaneous and point-mass.

problems.title: Integrate a prescribed time-varying stellar wind
problems.scenario: A hypothetical star starts at 35 solar masses. For the first million years it loses mass at 2×10⁻⁶ solar masses per year; for the next half-million years the prescribed loss rate is 6×10⁻⁶ solar masses per year.
problems.task: Compute the total wind mass lost and final mass; identify why this alone cannot determine the final black-hole remnant mass.
steps: The first interval loses (2×10⁻⁶)(10⁶)=2 solar masses.
The second loses (6×10⁻⁶)(0.5×10⁶)=3 solar masses.
Total prescribed wind loss is 5 solar masses; final toy stellar mass is 30 solar masses.
Remnant mass also depends on subsequent stellar evolution, collapse, fallback/ejecta, neutrino losses, binary interaction and the remnant prescription; wind integration alone does not specify it.
rubric: Each interval integrated with correct units

problems.title: Determine whether a donor fills its Roche lobe
problems.scenario: An idealized circular synchronized equal-mass binary has separation a=20 solar radii. The donor's radius is 8 solar radii. Use Eggleton's volume-equivalent Roche-lobe ratio R_L/a≈0.379 when q=1.
problems.task: Calculate R_L and the fractional overfill (R_d−R_L)/R_L. Does this prove that mass transfer will be unstable?
steps: The donor's approximate Roche radius is 0.379×20=7.58 solar radii.
Its radius exceeds the lobe by 8−7.58=0.42 solar radii.
The fractional geometric overfill is 0.42/7.58≈0.0554, or about 5.5%.
This indicates a toy geometric overflow condition, not a stability criterion; that additionally needs stellar structural and Roche-lobe responses during mass loss.

problems.title: Derive the sudden mass-loss disruption threshold
problems.scenario: A circular Newtonian pre-event relative orbit has initial gravitational parameter GM_i and separation r, so v_i²=GM_i/r. An instantaneous symmetric explosion removes gravitational mass without a natal kick or position change.
problems.task: Express the post-event specific orbital energy using f=M_lost/M_i. Derive the condition for an unbound post-event orbit and interpret the equality case.
steps: After the event GM_f=(1−f)GM_i while separation and relative speed are frozen in the impulse approximation.
ε_f=v_i²/2−GM_f/r=GM_i/(2r)−(1−f)GM_i/r=(GM_i/r)(f−1/2).
If f<1/2, ε_f<0 and the toy pair stays bound. At f=1/2, ε_f=0 (parabolic threshold); at f>1/2 it becomes unbound.
Specify that this half-mass threshold assumes an initially circular orbit, no kick, instantaneous symmetric loss and isolated point masses; it is not a universal disruption rule.
rubric: Bound, marginal and unbound cases distinguished

problems.title: Find eccentricity from a directional kick
problems.scenario: In post-event toy units, r=(1,0), GM_f=1 and v′=(0.3,0.8). Treat the orbit as Newtonian after the impulse, with no further drag.
problems.task: Calculate ε, specific angular momentum h and eccentricity e from e²=1+2εh²/(GM_f)². Distinguish the radial and tangential velocity contributions.
steps: Compute |v′|²=0.3²+0.8²=0.73, so ε=0.73/2−1=−0.635: the orbit is bound.
The cross product is h=|r×v′|=|1×0.8−0×0.3|=0.8; the radial component does not add instantaneous angular momentum.
A bound orbit's shape follows energy and angular momentum together; an energy sign alone does not specify eccentricity.
rubric: Angular momentum uses vector cross product

problems.title: Prove the fourth-power separation dependence of inspiral time
problems.scenario: For fixed component masses in a leading-order circular point-mass model, the orbit shrinks according to da/dt=−K/a³ with K>0 constant.
problems.task: Separate variables and integrate to the formal a=0 limit. Then compare the leading times at separations a and 1.5a.
steps: Rearrange dt=−a³da/K.
Integrating from a₀ to 0 gives t=(1/K)∫₀^a₀a³da=a₀⁴/(4K).
At the same masses, t(1.5a)/t(a)=1.5⁴=5.0625.
The integral extrapolates a weak-field leading approximation to zero separation; near merger, full strong-field and spin effects replace it.

problems.title: Estimate a strain-to-length scale without mistaking it for a detector output
problems.scenario: An idealized interferometer has an arm length of L=4 km, and a passing wave has characteristic dimensionless strain h=2×10⁻²¹. Assume favorable geometry and only calculate the order-of-magnitude scale hL.
problems.task: Convert the length into SI units, compute hL and explain why this simple number is not an actual calibrated detector measurement.
steps: Convert 4 km to 4000 m.
Multiply hL=(2×10⁻²¹)(4×10³ m)=8×10⁻¹⁸ m.
Strain is dimensionless, so the product has length units; the simple calculation is an order-of-magnitude differential displacement scale.
Real interferometers measure optical-phase response with frequency dependence, arm geometry, polarization, noise and calibration. One cannot claim a GW detection from hL alone.

problems.title: Calculate a weighted yield and effective sample size
problems.scenario: Three independently simulated toy binaries have outcome indicators (1,0,1) and nonnegative target-population weights (1,2,7). All weights use the same target-distribution convention.
problems.task: Calculate the raw successful-system fraction, normalized weighted fraction and N_eff=(Σw)²/Σw². Explain whether any of these is a physical merger rate.
steps: Two of three distinct systems succeed, giving an unweighted fraction 2/3.
The weighted successful sum is 1+7=8, while total weight is 1+2+7=10; the normalized weighted success fraction is 0.8.
The effective-size diagnostic is N_eff=10²/(1²+2²+7²)=100/54≈1.85; unequal weights concentrate information relative to three equal-weight draws.
A physical formation efficiency requires consistent represented formed-stellar-mass normalization; a cosmic merger rate additionally requires history and delays, and detections require selection.
rubric: No false identification with physical rate

problems.title: Separate Monte Carlo variation from modeling uncertainty
problems.scenario: You simulate N=400 independent Bernoulli toy systems under a fixed model and find that 100 meet a stated criterion. A second model has not yet been tested.
problems.task: Estimate p̂ and its plug-in binomial standard error. What happens to the standard error if the simulation size is quadrupled but the underlying success probability stays the same?
steps: The plug-in standard error is sqrt(0.25×0.75/400)=sqrt(0.00046875)≈0.02165, about 2.17 percentage points.
At N=1600 with the same underlying probability, standard error is halved to about 0.01083 because it scales as 1/√N.
Larger samples reduce sampling noise but do not correct a wrong kick prescription, selection function, dependence between samples or inconsistent sampling weights.

problems.title: Trace two stellar-birth cohorts into a delayed merger history
problems.scenario: In a toy cosmic-time model, 1000 solar masses of stars form at t=2 Gyr and 2000 solar masses form at t=5 Gyr. Formation efficiency is one merger-capable compact binary per 1000 solar masses, and each surviving system merges exactly 3 Gyr after stellar birth.
problems.task: Determine the merger epochs and counts and explain why a detected-event histogram would require additional conversions.
steps: The first cohort represents one merger-capable binary and the second two, under the specified toy efficiency.
Add the 3-Gyr delay to each birth time: the toy mergers occur at t=5 Gyr (one) and t=8 Gyr (two).
The intrinsic merger history is shifted relative to the two birth spikes even though their input star-formation counts are unchanged.
Cosmological volume, source/observer time conversion, source-parameter-dependent detection probabilities and observational exposure would be needed before predicting a detected histogram.
rubric: Both merger epochs and counts correct

problems.title: Why an observed majority need not be an intrinsic majority
problems.scenario: Class A makes up 30% of a hypothetical intrinsic compact-merger population and class B 70%. Class A has detection probability 0.9 while class B has probability 0.1 over the same toy observing window.
problems.task: Compute the expected detected class-A fraction and explain which ingredient must enter a population analysis before interpreting the observed class ratio.
steps: Expected detected fractions before renormalizing are 0.3×0.9=0.27 for A and 0.7×0.1=0.07 for B.
Total expected detected fraction is 0.34; among detections A contributes 0.27/0.34≈0.794, or 79.4%.
A would dominate the toy catalog even though its intrinsic share is only 30%. This alone does not determine a formation-channel fraction for a real dataset.
Population inference requires a forward likelihood with parameter-dependent detection selection and appropriate event measurement uncertainty, not a histogram of detected-event medians alone.
rubric: No astrophysical conclusions from toy assumptions

relationships.why: Orbital binding energy provides the post-explosion bound/unbound criterion.
Metallicity can change metal-line-driven wind strength under otherwise comparable massive-star conditions.
Stellar-wind mass loss changes the pre-collapse mass budget and can affect remnant masses in a specified model.
Filling an effective Roche boundary provides a geometric condition for overflow.
In some binary configurations unstable transfer can initiate common-envelope evolution.
Natal kicks change post-collapse relative velocity, survival and orbital elements, conditional on mass loss and kick orientation.
Chirp mass enters the leading-order frequency evolution and phase of a quasi-circular inspiral waveform.
Sampling initial binaries allows population synthesis to approximate distributions of evolutionary outcomes.
A formation-efficiency estimate must account for the sampled population's weights and normalization.
Earlier star formation contributes to mergers after the modeled formation-to-merger delay distribution.
Selection-aware normalization is required when inferring intrinsic properties from a detected catalog.
